Biological Sciences
BS 1000 - Plants and Society
Credits: 4
A one semester lecture/laboratory course in general botany for non-science majors. The course covers the principles of
plant anatomy and physiology, as well as the impact of plants and agriculture on society. Topics covered include the use
and history of plants as food, medicines, and poisons.
BS 2100 - Biology for Non-science Majors
Credits: 4
A one‑semester lecture/laboratory course in general biology for non-science majors. Surveys the major concepts and
principles of biology, including cell structure and function, genetics, ecology, diversity and evolution. Topics related to
the human experience are also discussed.
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Every semester.

This is a 4-credit, 2000-level lecture course designed for biology majors and non‑majors (including Public Health).
Students learn core biological foundations needed to understand foodborne illness and chemical hazards, including: (i) a
brief, accessible introduction to prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; (ii) basic human physiology relevant to digestion,
immunity, and inflammation; and (iii) how microbes, allergens, and selected contaminants affect human health across
the food chain. The course emphasizes public health reasoning, outbreak thinking, risk communication, and
evidence‑based decision making. Class meetings use case studies, guided data interpretation, and short applied
activities.
Prerequisites
None
BS 2300 - Anatomy and Physiology I Lecture
Credits: 3
This is the first semester of a two-semester sequence in which human anatomy and physiology are studied using a body
systems approach with emphasis on the interrelationships between form and function at the gross and microscopic
levels of organization. Demonstrating proficiency in this course is commonly required for entry into many Health
Professions Programs such as Physician’s Assistant, Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy, and Nursing just to name
a few. As such the course will be taught at a high level commensurate with ensuring such proficiency. Topics include;
basic anatomical and directional terminology, fundamental concepts and principles of cell biology, histology and in
depth study of the integumentary, skeletal, muscular and nervous systems.
Prerequisites
ECII and MA 1020
When Offered:
Every Semester

BS 2490 - Environmental Science
Credits: 4
The focus of this lecture course is on the interactions of humans with their environment. Human impact on the world’s
ecosystems is emphasized. The theme stressed throughout this course is that every system involving life is dependent
upon maintaining balances between nutrient gains and losses, between energy inflows and outflows, and between births
and deaths within populations. Against this background, various aspects of the human system, such as our use of soils,
our disposal of wastes, our use of resources, land, and energy and our population, are shown to be out of balance. The
consequences of these imbalances are discussed in relation to our political and economic system.
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Every Fall and Spring
BS 3300 - Biotechnology Workshop
Credits: 4
Designed to develop laboratory skills in the basic techniques used to study molecular genetics. Both prokaryotic and
eukaryotic organisms are used as models for the experiments. Some of the techniques introduced in the course include
DNA isolation, agarose gel electrophoresis, restriction enzymes, gene transfer, gene cloning, southern blot, PCR, RT-
PCR, and gene sequencing. In the latter part of the course, students will be introduced to the Human Genome Project
and to some of the techniques used in DNA sequencing and analysis.
Prerequisites
EMS
When Offered:
Occasionally.

BS 3450 - Plant Biology
Credits: 4
The study of plants as biological organisms. Topics include classification and evolution of the plant kingdom: plant
anatomy, physiology and reproduction, with emphasis on the flowering plants. Consideration given to experimental
methods used in studying plants and the importance of plants and plant studies. Students are expected to complete an
experimental project or observational study. Lecture, discussion, laboratory and field trips, or audio tutorial integration
of these are presented.
Prerequisites

BS 3500 - Invertebrate Zoology
Credits: 4
This lecture/laboratory course introduces the student to the diversity of form and function among the invertebrates
using a phylogenetic approach. It emphasizes their importance in ecology, diseases, food sources and as biomedical
models. Laboratory sessions include dissection of representative animals and encourage individual research projects.
Prerequisites

BS 3510 - Parasitology
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course. Major parasites of medical and economic interest are examined, including the causal agents
of malaria, trypanosomiasis schistosomiasis, and filariasis. The ecology, anatomy, pathology, and public health
importance of these parasites are emphasized. Laboratories include both live and prepared material.
Prerequisites
BS 2400 - BS 2410 with grades of “C” or better; EC II
BS 3520 - Comparative Anatomy
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course designed for biology majors and premedical students. Emphasis is on the basic anatomical
patterns of vertebrate structure. Morphogenesis and structure function relationships are discussed in terms of adaptive
significance. Laboratory includes dissections of aquatic and terrestrial vertebrates.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII

BS 3530 - Comparative Genomics

differences between organisms, how the genome is constructed and operates, and how genomes evolved. Understand
the advances in genomic technologies and their applications in health care. Lab sections will explore the latest
sequencing technologies and tools to analyze genomic data.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS2411 with a C or better, ECII

BS 3810 - Biological Aspects of Aging
Credits: 4
Lecture/workshop course designed for science students. Examines the aging process on the molecular, cellular, and
organismic levels. Emphasizes alterations during the aging process in cells whose life span is identical to that of the
entire organism. Examination of various pathological disorders in relationship to aging is also emphasized. Students are
required to read original articles and be prepared to discuss current topics in workshop settings. Completion of BS3400

Credits: 4

infectious diseases or cancer, and it will describe in detail the cells and molecules of the mammalian immune system.
The laboratory component is a research-based course where students participate in the development of new knowledge
by generating a novel research question and performing their own experimental design. Completion of CP 2120 and BS
4400 or BS 4460 is recommended.

BS 4470 - Ecology
Credits: 4
A general ecology course focused on the study of ecosystems. It fulfills the population content area course requirement
for the BA and BS degrees in Biology. The course includes a lecture (3 hours/week) and a laboratory component (3
hours/week). Topics include ecosystem structure and function, population dynamics, community structure, food webs,
energy flow, nutrient cycles, biogeography, associations, succession, adaptation and niche analysis, and interspecific
interactions. The course is taught in a blended format with a significant online course component. The laboratory
component includes extensive field work. Students working in groups must design and implement a research project
involving data collection from a campus ecosystem. The project culminates in a group oral presentation. Students are
also encouraged to present their results at a local or regional conference and/or submit their results for publication to a
peer-reviewed undergraduate research journal
Prerequisites
Bs 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, and BS 2411 with a grade of C or better; ECII

BS 4500 - Neurobiology
Credits: 4
Lecture course designed to familiarize students with cellular mechanisms within the nervous system and how they are
used to promote intercellular communication. Connecting molecular signaling to higher-order neurobiological function
will be a large focus of the course. Includes concepts as they relate to neurobiology such as synaptic transmission,
neuroplasticity, neuronal development, sensory systems, neuropharmacology, drugs of abuse, and
neurodegenerative/neurodevelopmental disorders. Students will prepare a research project utilizing primary scientific
literature and will be expected to convey this information via writing. Completion of BS 4400 is recommended.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:

BS 4550 - Cancer Cell Biology
Credits: 4
Lecture/Discussion. The study of cancer disease requires knowledge of several essential biological processes that govern
the basic of the living system. This course will explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying cancer
development with the aim of understanding how changes in the normal cell growth and division processes lead to the
formation of tumors. Case studies will be used to explore the roles of specific mutations in cancer develop- ment and the
pathways they affect, as well as the classes of genes targeted during cancer development. This upper level course builds
on concepts introduced in courses in Cell Biology and Genetics and will emphasize experimental methods and design as
well as critical data analysis. Students will discuss papers from the primary literature each week individually or in
groups. Completion of BS 4400 or BS 4460 is recommended.
Prerequisites

BS 4680 - Environmental Health
Credits: 4
This course takes an integrated approach to the development of a basic understanding of the impact of the environment
on health. It examines chronic and infectious diseases in relation to modern life styles. A new section examines the AIDS
epidemic in relation to the environment. Other topics that are covered include: air pollution in the general industrial
environment; water pollution; the effects of pesticides and food additives; synthetic organic chemicals such as PCB’s and
dioxins as environmental estrogens; health effects of radiation and safety of nuclear energy. Satisfies elective
requirement for B.A. in Biology.
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
On demand.
BS 5400 - Senior Seminar
Credits: 4
Senior Seminar in Biology is designed to promote an in-depth consideration of special topics in current biological
research. The student will, under the advisement of a faculty mentor, develop a topic as a library study and present the
results both orally and as a written paper. The process of writing this paper will consist of a series of tasks that must be
completed in order. The course will also include presentations by external speakers, and students will be asked to read
papers of these speakers, draft questions to ask the speakers, and to write short commentary in regard to each
speaker. This course is intended to be taken in the final semester before graduation. Student eligibility will be
determined by faculty review.
Prerequisites
None, requires permission of instructor or Chair to register

records.title: Plants and Society
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A one semester lecture/laboratory course in general botany for non-science majors. The course covers the principles of
plant anatomy and physiology, as well as the impact of plants and agriculture on society. Topics covered include the use
and history of plants as food, medicines, and poisons.

records.title: Biology for Non-science Majors
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A one‑semester lecture/laboratory course in general biology for non-science majors. Surveys the major concepts and
principles of biology, including cell structure and function, genetics, ecology, diversity and evolution. Topics related to
the human experience are also discussed.
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Food Safety: From Farm to Fork
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

This is a 4-credit, 2000-level lecture course designed for biology majors and non‑majors (including Public Health).
Students learn core biological foundations needed to understand foodborne illness and chemical hazards, including: (i) a
brief, accessible introduction to prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; (ii) basic human physiology relevant to digestion,
immunity, and inflammation; and (iii) how microbes, allergens, and selected contaminants affect human health across
the food chain. The course emphasizes public health reasoning, outbreak thinking, risk communication, and
evidence‑based decision making. Class meetings use case studies, guided data interpretation, and short applied
activities.
Prerequisites
None

records.title: Anatomy and Physiology I Lecture
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
This is the first semester of a two-semester sequence in which human anatomy and physiology are studied using a body
systems approach with emphasis on the interrelationships between form and function at the gross and microscopic
levels of organization. Demonstrating proficiency in this course is commonly required for entry into many Health
Professions Programs such as Physician’s Assistant, Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy, and Nursing just to name
a few. As such the course will be taught at a high level commensurate with ensuring such proficiency. Topics include;
basic anatomical and directional terminology, fundamental concepts and principles of cell biology, histology and in
depth study of the integumentary, skeletal, muscular and nervous systems.
Prerequisites
ECII and MA 1020
When Offered:
Every Semester

records.title: Anatomy and Physiology I Laboratory
records.sourceText:
Credits: 1

This course is the laboratory component for BS 2300 - Anatomy and Physiology I Lecture
. Demonstrating proficiency in this course is commonly required for entry into many Health Professions Programs such
as Physician’s Assistant, Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy, and Nursing just to name a few. As such the course
will be taught at a high level commensurate with ensuring such proficiency. It covers the study of anatomical and
directional terminology, fundamental concepts and principles of cell biology, histology and in depth study of the
integumentary, skeletal, muscular and nervous systems using an experimental approach complemented with the use of
preserved mammalian organisms as well as models.
Prerequisites
ECII and MA 1020
When Offered:
Every Semester

records.title: Anatomy and Physiology II Lecture
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
This is the second semester of a two-semester sequence in which human anatomy and physiology are studied using a
body systems approach with emphasis on the interrelationships between form and function at the gross and microscopic
levels of organization. Demonstrating proficiency in this course is commonly required for entry into many Health
Professions Programs such as Physician’s Assistant, Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy, and Nursing just to name
a few. As such the course will be taught at a high level commensurate with ensuring such proficiency. Topics include; in
depth study of the endocrine system, digestive system, metabolism, nutrition, respiratory system, cardiovascular
system, lymphatic system and immunity, urinary system, fluid/electrolyte and acid/base balance, and the male and
female reproductive systems.
Prerequisites
BS 2300 and BS 2301 with a C or better

records.title: Anatomy and Physiology II Laboratory
records.sourceText:
Credits: 1

This course is the laboratory component for BS 2310 - Anatomy and Physiology II Lecture
. Demonstrating proficiency in this course is commonly required for entry into many Health Professions Programs such
as Physician’s Assistant, Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy, and Nursing just to name a few. As such the course
will be taught at a high level commensurate with ensuring such proficiency. It covers the in depth study of the endocrine
system, digestive system, metabolism, nutrition, respiratory system, cardiovascular system, lymphatic system and
immunity, urinary system, fluid/electrolyte and acid/base balance, and the male and female reproductive systems.
These topics will be covered using an experimental approach complemented with the use of preserved mammalian
organisms as well as models.
Prerequisites
BS 2300 and BS 2301 with a C or better
When Offered:
Every Semester

records.title: Basic Biosciences I
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
First semester of freshman biology courses covering content areas including molecular and cellular biology, genetics,
genomics and evolution.
Prerequisites

Every Semester

records.sourceText:
Credits: 1
First semester of freshman biology laboratory courses covering content areas including molecular and cellular biology,
genetics, genomics and evolution.

records.title: Basic Biosciences II
records.sourceText:

Second semester of freshman biology courses covering content areas including cell metabolism, comparative animal and
plant anatomy and physiology and ecology.

BS 2400 and BS 2401 with a C or better; MA 1020 or math proficiencyCorequisite BS 2411 if taken for the first
timePrerequisite/Corequisite

records.sourceText:
Credits: 1
Second semester of freshman biology laboratory courses covering content areas including cell metabolism, comparative
animal and plant anatomy and physiology and ecology.

records.title: Environmental Science
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The focus of this lecture course is on the interactions of humans with their environment. Human impact on the world’s
ecosystems is emphasized. The theme stressed throughout this course is that every system involving life is dependent
upon maintaining balances between nutrient gains and losses, between energy inflows and outflows, and between births
and deaths within populations. Against this background, various aspects of the human system, such as our use of soils,
our disposal of wastes, our use of resources, land, and energy and our population, are shown to be out of balance. The
consequences of these imbalances are discussed in relation to our political and economic system.
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Every Fall and Spring

records.title: Biotechnology Workshop
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Designed to develop laboratory skills in the basic techniques used to study molecular genetics. Both prokaryotic and
eukaryotic organisms are used as models for the experiments. Some of the techniques introduced in the course include
DNA isolation, agarose gel electrophoresis, restriction enzymes, gene transfer, gene cloning, southern blot, PCR, RT-
PCR, and gene sequencing. In the latter part of the course, students will be introduced to the Human Genome Project
and to some of the techniques used in DNA sequencing and analysis.
Prerequisites
EMS
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Vertebrate Physiology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

A regulatory systems approach to the principles of animal physiology, developed through consideration of functioning
of cells, tissues, and organ systems with an emphasis on humans. (With 3-hour laboratory)
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better; CP 2120 and CP 2121 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every semester

records.title: Plant Biology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The study of plants as biological organisms. Topics include classification and evolution of the plant kingdom: plant
anatomy, physiology and reproduction, with emphasis on the flowering plants. Consideration given to experimental
methods used in studying plants and the importance of plants and plant studies. Students are expected to complete an
experimental project or observational study. Lecture, discussion, laboratory and field trips, or audio tutorial integration
of these are presented.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better, ECII
When Offered:
Every Fall

records.title: Invertebrate Zoology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This lecture/laboratory course introduces the student to the diversity of form and function among the invertebrates
using a phylogenetic approach. It emphasizes their importance in ecology, diseases, food sources and as biomedical
models. Laboratory sessions include dissection of representative animals and encourage individual research projects.
Prerequisites

records.title: BS 2410 completed with grades of “C” or better
Parasitology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course. Major parasites of medical and economic interest are examined, including the causal agents
of malaria, trypanosomiasis schistosomiasis, and filariasis. The ecology, anatomy, pathology, and public health
importance of these parasites are emphasized. Laboratories include both live and prepared material.
Prerequisites

records.title: BS 2410 with grades of “C” or better; EC II
Comparative Anatomy
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course designed for biology majors and premedical students. Emphasis is on the basic anatomical
patterns of vertebrate structure. Morphogenesis and structure function relationships are discussed in terms of adaptive
significance. Laboratory includes dissections of aquatic and terrestrial vertebrates.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Fall

records.title: Comparative Genomics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course. Explore the interdisciplinary field of genome science. Study the genomic similarities and
differences between organisms, how the genome is constructed and operates, and how genomes evolved. Understand
the advances in genomic technologies and their applications in health care. Lab sections will explore the latest
sequencing technologies and tools to analyze genomic data.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS2411 with a C or better, ECII

When Offered:
Every FallNote:
This course is the combined comparative genomics lecture and lab, and is part of the Biological Sciences BA/BS and
Bioinformatics and Computational Biology BS. These degrees will be updated to reflect the combined lecture/lab.

records.title: Comparative Genomics Lab
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course. Explore the interdisciplinary field of genome science. Study the genomic similarities and
differences between organisms, how the genome is constructed and operates, and how genomes evolved. Understand
the advances in genomic technologies and their applications in health care. Lab sections will explore the latest
sequencing technologies and tools to analyze genomic data.
Prerequisites
BS 2400/BS 2401 andBS 2410/BS 2411 with grade of “C” or better.
When Offered:
Every other semester.

records.title: Biological Aspects of Aging
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/workshop course designed for science students. Examines the aging process on the molecular, cellular, and
organismic levels. Emphasizes alterations during the aging process in cells whose life span is identical to that of the
entire organism. Examination of various pathological disorders in relationship to aging is also emphasized. Students are
required to read original articles and be prepared to discuss current topics in workshop settings. Completion of BS3400
is recommended prior to enrolling in this course.
Prerequisites
BS2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better, ECII
When Offered:
Every Spring.

records.title: Intro to Bioinformatics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course. Explore the application of computer science tools to address biological questions through
lectures and labs. Survey the genomic and biomolecular databases and web bioinformatics resources. Understand the
algorithms and learn basic programming languages to analyze DNA, RNA, and proteins. Apply bioinformatics tools to
analyze real-world problems and data.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Spring

records.title: Cell Biology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/discussion/laboratory course whose content is directed to the study of the molecular basis of cell activities, cell
ultra structure, and its integration with cellular function. Lectures survey the cell in its environment, energy
transformation, mobility, replication of genetic material, growth, nucleocytoplasmic interactions. The laboratory
explores techniques used in the study of the cell.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Fall and Spring

records.title: Histology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A laboratory‑oriented course dealing with the microscopic and ultramicroscopic anatomy of mammalian tissues and
organs with emphasis on relating structure to function.

Prerequisites
BS2400, BS2401, BS2410, BS2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Fall

records.title: Microbiology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course concerned with structure-function relationships in various types of microorganisms, with
particular emphasis on bacteria. Nutrition, biosynthesis, energetics, growth, microbial interactions and symbiotic
relationships, host-parasite relationships, and microbial genetics are among the topics discussed.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS2401, BS2410, and BS2411 with a grade of “C” or better; EC Il

records.title: Developmental Biology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A lecture/laboratory course covering fundamental principles of developmental biology. Topics included: gametogenesis,
fertilization, cleavage, gastrulation, growth and differentiation. This course attempts to integrate the descriptive,
experimental and genetic approaches to the study of developmental biology. Completion of BS 3520 is recommended.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Spring

records.title: Evolution
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

Lecture/discussion course presenting the history of life on earth from its inception to the emergence and early history of
Homo sapiens. Through readings, lectures, demonstrations, laboratories, discussions, and museum trips, students
examine modern evolutionary theory and concepts, including abiogenesis, adaptation, population genetics, race,
speciation, and progressive evolution. Completion of BS4460 is recommended.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS2410, and BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Fall and Spring

records.title: Genetics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course presenting the fundamental principles of genetics, the molecular biology of the gene, and
heredity in humans. Through lectures, readings, laboratories, and discussions, students examine the experimental
evidence leading to currently accepted concepts, and critically analyze the implications of various findings in human
genetics.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, and BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Fall and Spring

records.title: Immunology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/laboratory course. This course will introduce students to the essential concepts of how the immune system
works, what are the molecular and cellular mechanisms and pathways involved in the defense of an organism from
infectious diseases or cancer, and it will describe in detail the cells and molecules of the mammalian immune system.
The laboratory component is a research-based course where students participate in the development of new knowledge
by generating a novel research question and performing their own experimental design. Completion of CP 2120 and BS
4400 or BS 4460 is recommended.

Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, and BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Occasionally

records.title: Ecology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A general ecology course focused on the study of ecosystems. It fulfills the population content area course requirement
for the BA and BS degrees in Biology. The course includes a lecture (3 hours/week) and a laboratory component (3
hours/week). Topics include ecosystem structure and function, population dynamics, community structure, food webs,
energy flow, nutrient cycles, biogeography, associations, succession, adaptation and niche analysis, and interspecific
interactions. The course is taught in a blended format with a significant online course component. The laboratory
component includes extensive field work. Students working in groups must design and implement a research project
involving data collection from a campus ecosystem. The project culminates in a group oral presentation. Students are
also encouraged to present their results at a local or regional conference and/or submit their results for publication to a
peer-reviewed undergraduate research journal
Prerequisites
Bs 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, and BS 2411 with a grade of C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Fall

records.title: Microbial Ecology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is designed to introduce students to the study of microbial ecosystems its structure and function using an
applied learning research approach modeling the scientific research process. Students should be aware this course
requires a significant amount of independent work. In the lecture component students will be introduced to ecological
theory to support the laboratory experimentation. As part of their investigation the students will learn about ecosystem
structure, i.e. biotic and abiotic components, and function, i.e. symbiotic interactions and food webs. As part of the biotic

component of the ecosystem, the students will focus on the study of a microbiome using both traditional microbiology
and next generation sequencing methodology, i.e. microscopy, isolation using generalized and selective media, and
molecular techniques: DNA isolation from environmental samples, PCR amplification using specific primers, i.e. 16S
rDNA, and sequence analysis. This course fulfills the population core requirement for the BA and BS in Biology, and can
also be used as one of the upper division biology course requirement in the BS in Bioinformatics and Computational
Biology. This course is recommended for students who plan to pursue a career in basic science or biomedical research,
and the health profession. Prerequisite: BS2400/BS2401-2410/BS2411 with a grade of C or better.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, and BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Spring

records.title: Animal Behavior
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A lecture/laboratory course introducing the field of animal behavior. Lectures, discussions and films explore topics
including the cultural basis of behavior, the organization and physiology of the nervous system and its role in
controlling behavior, the endocrine basis of behavior, genetic basis of behavior and sociobiology.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, and BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Occasionally

records.title: Human Ecology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Students will examine the adaptation of human populations to their environment. Topics include: biological and cultural
evolution, human diversity, impact of limiting resources, the ecology of disease, and urban ecology and planning.
Prerequisites

BS 2400/BS 2401 and BS 2410/BS 2411 with grades of “C” or better
When Offered:
This course is offered once a year.

records.title: Neurobiology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture course designed to familiarize students with cellular mechanisms within the nervous system and how they are
used to promote intercellular communication. Connecting molecular signaling to higher-order neurobiological function
will be a large focus of the course. Includes concepts as they relate to neurobiology such as synaptic transmission,
neuroplasticity, neuronal development, sensory systems, neuropharmacology, drugs of abuse, and
neurodegenerative/neurodevelopmental disorders. Students will prepare a research project utilizing primary scientific
literature and will be expected to convey this information via writing. Completion of BS 4400 is recommended.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Fall, every other year.

records.title: Cancer Cell Biology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/Discussion. The study of cancer disease requires knowledge of several essential biological processes that govern
the basic of the living system. This course will explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying cancer
development with the aim of understanding how changes in the normal cell growth and division processes lead to the
formation of tumors. Case studies will be used to explore the roles of specific mutations in cancer develop- ment and the
pathways they affect, as well as the classes of genes targeted during cancer development. This upper level course builds
on concepts introduced in courses in Cell Biology and Genetics and will emphasize experimental methods and design as
well as critical data analysis. Students will discuss papers from the primary literature each week individually or in
groups. Completion of BS 4400 or BS 4460 is recommended.
Prerequisites

BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, and BS 2411 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Occasionally

records.title: Molecular Biology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Lecture/Laboratory course to introduce students to both the theoretical and practical aspects of molecular biology. An
understanding of molecular biology necessitates a synthesis of information from genetics, biochemistry, cell biology,
physics and chemistry. The course will include microbial studies, cellular components, genes, regulation etc. The lab
component will utilize techniques of genetic engineering.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, and BS 2411 with a C or better; CP 2120 with a C or better; ECII
When Offered:
Every Spring

records.title: Pharmacology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A lecture/readings course dealing with the principles of drug interactions in animal cells and tissues. The molecular
level of pharmacological actions and their subsequent impact on behavioral and physiological functions are studied.
Students are required to read primary scientific literature and are expected to be able to convey the information
contained within through writing. This course is intended for students who plan for a career in a variety of fields,
ranging from allied health professions through basic science research.
Prerequisites
BS 2400, BS 2401, BS 2410, BS2411 with a C or better, ECII
When Offered:
OtherNote:

This course has run three times so far, and already is in Banner and DegreeWorks. It is not present in the course catalog
and this is to rectify that discrepancy.

records.title: Environmental Health
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course takes an integrated approach to the development of a basic understanding of the impact of the environment
on health. It examines chronic and infectious diseases in relation to modern life styles. A new section examines the AIDS
epidemic in relation to the environment. Other topics that are covered include: air pollution in the general industrial
environment; water pollution; the effects of pesticides and food additives; synthetic organic chemicals such as PCB’s and
dioxins as environmental estrogens; health effects of radiation and safety of nuclear energy. Satisfies elective
requirement for B.A. in Biology.
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
On demand.

records.title: Senior Seminar
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Senior Seminar in Biology is designed to promote an in-depth consideration of special topics in current biological
research. The student will, under the advisement of a faculty mentor, develop a topic as a library study and present the
results both orally and as a written paper. The process of writing this paper will consist of a series of tasks that must be
completed in order. The course will also include presentations by external speakers, and students will be asked to read
papers of these speakers, draft questions to ask the speakers, and to write short commentary in regard to each
speaker. This course is intended to be taken in the final semester before graduation. Student eligibility will be
determined by faculty review.
Prerequisites
None, requires permission of instructor or Chair to register
When Offered:

Every SemesterNote:
Senior Seminar has already run in Fall 2024, and is in Banner and DegreeWorks. This is to update the active course
catalog.
This course is intended to be taken in the final semester before graduation. Students are individually screened by faculty
before registering for the course to determine eligibility.

records.title: Seminar I in Biology: Reading in the Discipline
records.sourceText:
Credits: 2
Designed to increase ability to read in the discipline. Students will survey scientific literature, learn how to research
topics, prepare abstracts, etc. Students will select a mentor and topic for Seminar II. Must be taken by students two
semesters prior to graduation.
Prerequisites
85-90 credits and permission of instructor
When Offered:
Every Fall and Spring.

records.title: Seminar II in Biology: Writing in the Discipline
records.sourceText:
Credits: 2
Designed to promote an in-depth consideration of special topics in current biological research. The course will include
presentations by both external speakers and students. The student will, under the advisement of a faculty mentor,
develop a topic either as a library or laboratory study and present the results both orally and as a written paper.
Prerequisites
BS 5410
When Offered:
Every Fall and Spring.

records.title: Advanced Research
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

Research project carried out under the supervision of a faculty member. Each project includes a survey of the
appropriate original literature and investigation of a selected research topic by experimental or theoretical methods.
Open to students of upper‑division standing, preferably seniors, on acceptance as a research student by a faculty
member. Students may take this course twice for credit but may receive only 4 credits from this course toward the major.
Grading will be CR/NC.
Prerequisites

records.title: BS 2410 with grades of “C” or better; permission of instructor
records.sourceText:
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Environmental Research
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Research project in environmental science carried out under supervision of a faculty member. Open to upper‑division
students, preferably seniors on acceptance as a research student by a faculty member.
Prerequisites

records.title: BS 2410 with grades of “C” or better; 3 upper‑division Biology courses; permission of instructor
records.sourceText:
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Biological Pharmacology
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
A lecture/readings course dealing with the priciples of drug interactions in animal cells and tissues. The molecular and
behavioral levels of pharmacological actions with impact on physiological functions are studied. Substance abuse issues
will be highlighted.
Prerequisites

Successful completion of the core science courses with a grade of B or better. (BS 4400 or BS4460 and BS 3400 or BS3520.

Independent study is to be carried out under the supervision of a faculty member. It permits students to investigate
areas that are not part of existing offerings.
